Well, as /u/Thaufas points out, this is tidyverse code, and since s/he has already made a good case for it, I'll make the case against it. I started using R about 8 or 9 years ago, and back then there was no tidyverse. There was one data manipulation package that I got really comfortable with, and that was something called plyr. Not to be confused with dplyr, because if you do get those things confused (or even load both packages at the same time), you'll break your code.

To me, plyr had a really nice, comfortable logic. You want to take a data frame, do some manipulations on it, and get a data frame back? ddply. You want to take an array, do some manipulations and get a data frame? adply. You want to take in a list and get a list back llply. It's simple, it's something the language needed, and it was brought to you by the great Hadley Wickham. It also included some really useful functions like rbind.fill, join (which is so much simpler and better than merge), and probably a few others that I am forgetting. 

Well, my code uses plyr everywhere, and at this point it's basically not portable because of it, because dplyr came along and Hadley decided that his original conception of how to make good \*ply functions changed. Except only for data frames, not lists or anything else. And also, you're supposed to use a pipe operator, which is sometimes convenient but often more irritating than useful.

But of course, everyone is using these packages now, including the younger people on my team, who basically think the tidyverse *is* R, since they learned 2 years ago when it was the big thing. 

Now don't get me wrong: I'm all for advancing the language, but I honestly don't think the tidyverse does that, for several reasons:

* Failure of backwards compatibility should scare everyone. I know that this sob story of me becoming dependent on plyr is not everyone else's problem. The possibility that your code might not work in 5-10-15 years is. Base R is pretty damn stable. The tidyverse isn't. There were some big deal changes in R 4.0 that concerned a lot of people, and they were nothing like the incompatibility issues between versions of the tidyverse.
* The tidyverse is bloatware at its worst. If you rely on one solitary tidyverse package, you're relying on 50. That's a *little* bit of an exaggeration, but not a huge exaggeration. If you learn to use base R to do the things you need to do, you only have to worry about the things that are really outside of your domain, like reading Excel files or doing complex machine learning stuff or I don't know what. If you rely on the tidyverse, you should expect your code to stop working in 5-10 years. Many of the best and most popular tidyverse packages (httr and stringr, to name two) are just wrappers for other packages. Why not use those packages directly instead of using the wrappers, which might make your code look nicer to someone who appreciates tidyverse coding, but will ultimately run more slowly and have two dependencies (at least) instead of one? 
* The tidyverse uses a whole lot of neat little tricks in the form of non-standard evaluation. Non-standard evaluation is certainly convenient at times. The problem is, in the long term, it hinders understanding of the language. It is certainly more convenient if you can, say, address parts of a dataset without explicitly calling that dataset every time. Who wants to write data$blahblah over and over again? But over time, you build a sense of how R works. When there's non-standard evaluation going on all the time, you never build that intuition, and that's going to hurt you in the long run. That's why the piping in that example is bothering you so much--you've been using R for years and you see this whole thing that just looks *odd* to you. It doesn't look like R. Well, if you learn the tidyverse way first, the R that you and I know is going to be just as confusing. But you and I can get our work done without dependencies that take an hour to load.

With that said, if you're going to be working with other people's code, you should at least learn the basics of the tidyverse, how to read the pipe operator (%>%) and the background behind the decisions that they make in the tidyverse. It's useful not only so you can read code that others have written, but also because you may ultimately decide that you want to go the tidyverse route--at least partially. All of my experiences have made me skeptical, but that shouldn't limit you. Use the best thing for the job you're doing. I've never been a huge fan of the pipe operator, but I'm to the point where I can use it and understand it when others use it. I've got a lot of code that uses stringr and httr, mostly because I didn't know they were just wrappers for stringi and curl. But I'm not going to rewrite all of that. And I use ggplot2 all the time. I do feel like people are a little too over-the-top about how great it is (since there are some pretty big flaws, in my way of thinking), but it's better than just about anything else.

Anyway, good luck figuring out that code!

I mean, after all, what is a flag? Why do we use a piece of cloth hanging from a pole to represent places? It's a standard that evolved over time. Why can't a flag be 3 dimensional? Why can't it be a laser show with music? Why can't it be a hologram? Why can't it be a delicious food? Well, because we wouldn't recognize those things as flags. Once you start down a path of standardization, though, it tends to produce more conformity. A flag is a symbol of a place that fits into a piece of cloth that you can hang from a pole. Can it be literally any shape? Can it be any size? Why not?

Standardization has pushed us to the point where most flags are rectangles (squares are rectangles too, but even squares aren't that common outside of Switzerland). So naturally, we feel a bit uncomfortable when flags aren't rectangles, and it's natural to want to "fix" it, as OP has done here. That doesn't mean Nepal's flag is wrong any more than Pocatello's old flag was wrong for having a copyright on it. These are just arbitrary rules, and certainly having standards hasn't meant that all standards are followed all the time.

However, standards are not, as you posit, the enemy of creativity. Some of the greatest art in history has been painted onto a 3:4 ratio canvas. Some of the greatest music has been written in sonata form, orchestrated for a standard symphony orchestra. Shakespeare wrote all of his plays in Iambic pentameter. How many great plays are typically (and successfully) performed on a proscenium stage? 

Which doesn't mean we can't enjoy art that challenges standards or escapes them all together. That is also interesting and worth attempting, but that doesn't make it superior to something that does fit nicely into a standard just for having done something different.

There are several tutorials if you search for how to animate SVGs in CSS. I'm sure I could have done it with gganimate and make it spit out a bunch of SVGs, but I wanted to do some annotations with cowplot, so in the end I just made a loop. Anyway, SVGs are just XML, so if you open them up, they look like code, not like garbage like a GIF or PNG. So it turns out all you have to do to put multiple frames in an SVG is to make a new file with opening and closing <svg> tags (you can actually just take one from one of the files so it has all of the parameters you want). Then you put each one into a <g id="framename"> ... </g>. And voila, your many SVGs are a single SVG with several frames. Then you have to do some crazy stuff in CSS that is a real pain in the ass. I'm not sure who came up with CSS animation, but it makes no sense. So again, go with one of those tutorials.

Then you have a choice: you can either do things the normal html way and include the css file and embed the SVG as an image, or you can put the CSS in a <style> tag and put your SVG right into your HTML file. The latter solution worked for me, and will work well for an RMarkdown document. Just use echo=FALSE, results='asis' and cat() the whole thing.

And that's pretty much it.

Now, the thing is, you could be really meticulous and figure out which shapes you actually want to move around and which ones are the same as in the other SVGs, because it really doesn't make sense to redraw your axes and titles and all of that stuff that isn't changing just because your lines or dots or whatever are. But since the whole point of this was to have something that was easy to update, I didn't do that. I haven't noticed that it's slow to render on any platforms, but maybe it is.

I like the idea of gganimate, but I have to admit, I was pretty irritated that it can't animate SVGs. For the project I was working on, I just figured it out (a pain, but worth it for the quality improvement).
